answer:
**Membership inference asks whether one particular record helped train the model.** It does not necessarily recover the record itself or the model's weights. An attacker may exploit lower loss or higher confidence on training examples than on otherwise similar unseen examples. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.05820)

Suppose a model gives unusually confident answers on a rare sentence it memorized. An attacker with that sentence and query access may compare its behavior with a reference distribution and infer membership. Attack strength depends on outputs available, auxiliary data, and the training process.

**A fair evaluation must match member and nonmember distributions.** If members come from one domain and nonmembers from another, the attack may merely recognize the domain. Use realistic candidate records and report false-positive rates, especially for rare or sensitive subgroups.

Regularization and output restrictions can reduce some attacks but do not certify privacy. Proper differential privacy provides a formal influence bound under stated assumptions. Distinguish the privacy question from ordinary generalization: good average test accuracy does not rule out memorization of a small sensitive subset.

**Technical details and references.**

Membership inference tries to determine whether a specific record was in training, using model outputs, losses, gradients, or other access. A model may behave more confidently on memorized training examples than comparable nonmembers. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.05820)

Assess a defined attacker, access level, and realistic member/nonmember distribution; distribution mismatch can make an attack look stronger than true membership leakage. Regularization and output restriction may reduce risk but do not certify privacy. Properly implemented differential privacy offers a formal influence bound. Evaluate sensitive subgroups and rare examples, and distinguish membership inference from reconstructing the full record or extracting model weights.
